Chapter One

The first time Mirzapur Road moved on my map, I blamed the heat.

The room above the Government Printing Press was a long, low box of a place, smelling of lampblack, pumice, and the particular stale sweetness of paper left too long in the sun. It was the third week of June, 1893, and Kolkata still wore Calcutta in its ledgers. The ceiling fan clicked in its slow circle. Outside, a water-carrier called for water in a voice that sounded like it had been dragged down a well. On the board before me, the new map of North Kolkata lay pinned at its four corners, a blue-white sheet of paper no bigger than a dining table.

My map was nearly finished. I had been hired to redraw the quarter between College Street and the old fish market for the drainage survey, a job considered too delicate for a junior draughtsman and too dull for a senior one. My father had been a leveller in the Bengal Survey. He died leaving me a theodolite, a set of brass dividers, and the conviction that if a thing would not stand still, it had not been measured carefully enough. I had measured Mirzapur Road twice. I had checked its bearing against the old plans, its width against the footnotes in my father’s field book, its corners against the positions of three temples, a clockmaker’s shop, and the back gate of the Serampore Mission house.

At five o’clock I had inked the final line in India ink. I had let it dry under a blotter. I had trimmed the lamp. At eleven o’clock, when I looked up from copying a contour line, Mirzapur Road stood six millimetres to the north of where I had left it.

I touched the table. The board was steady. I touched the map. The paper was smooth, taut, unmarked. The ink was dry. I lifted my dividers and measured from the fixed line of College Street to the moved line of Mirzapur. Six millimetres. I measured again. Six millimetres. I looked at the four brass pins. They were in the same holes. I looked at my hand. It was open, empty, and very clean.

Then I did what my father would have done. I stopped being frightened and began taking notes.

By twelve, Mr. Hartley had found his way up from the lower office with a tin cup of Assam tea and the look of a man who expected trouble to be his. He was an assistant surveyor, a small Englishman with a mustache that tried to look important and usually failed. He set the cup down on my T-square. I moved it.

“You have lost the scale, Amala,” he said.

“No, sir.”

“You have. That whole block is leaning.”

“Only Mirzapur Road is leaning, sir. The rest of the city is exactly where I put it.”

He leaned over the sheet. The lamp flared between us. I saw his mouth tighten. When a man like Mr. Hartley saw something he did not like, he made it smaller.

“The paper has curled,” he said.

“The paper is pinned at four corners.”

“Heat does strange things.”

“It is June, sir. It does strange things every day. But it has not moved a single house, a single lane, or a single temple on this map. It has moved Mirzapur Road.”

He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, in the tone he used when he meant to be kind and succeeded only in being tired, “A street does not move, Miss Roy.”

“Not yet,” I said.

He stared at me. I would have given a good deal to unsay it. But the words were in the room already, and the lamp oil smelt sharper than before.

Dwarkanath Sen, the old clerk, came in with the field book. He had a face full of folds, like a map that had been folded and unfolded so often it had begun to hold creases for their own sake. He put the book on the board and opened it to Mirzapur.

“The old survey put the road here,” he said, tapping a line in the margin. “Three houses south of where you have it now. But the houses are where they have always been. The fishmonger is at the same corner. The clockmaker has the same broken window. The road is where you see it.”

“Is it?” I asked. “Have you walked it this week?”

“Why would I walk a road?”

“Because you are telling me it is still there.”

He looked at me as if I had suggested he walk into the Ganges. “It is a road, Miss Roy. Roads are not things you lose.”

“Then perhaps it is something else,” I said. “Something that has learned to be a road.”

I sent him away with the old plans and an order to fetch the 1878 proof copies from the lower vault. I told Mr. Hartley I needed to compare the sheet with the original tracings. He gave me a look that said he would be back before I had time to invent a second impossibility, and then he was gone, his boots tapping softly on the stairs.

When I was alone, I took a fine pencil and made four small crosses on the board, exactly outside the four corners of the map. I put my brass ruler across Mirzapur Road and left it there. Then I walked down to the tea room, drank two cups of strong black tea, and listened to the printer’s boys argue about cricket.

When I came up, the ruler was where I had left it. Mirzapur Road had moved another four millimetres east. The line passed through the shadow of the ruler as if the ruler had been a window and the street a bird. I wrote the time in my notebook: 1:17. I wrote the distance: four millimetres. I wrote the direction: east by north. I wrote, in letters so small they looked like insects, “It is not the paper.”

The second night it moved again. The third night, I did not go down for tea. I stayed in the room with the door barred, the lamp burning, and a cup of cold water on the table. At one o’clock I heard it. I had thought it was the street, but I had not known the street made a sound. It was not a footstep. It was not a wheel. It was a soft scraping, like the slow passage of a chisel across wet plaster, and it came from under the floor, from the wall, from the paper itself. I looked down. Mirzapur Road was sliding a little to the south, toward the line of Bakergunge Street. I did not breathe. I laid both hands flat on the map, as one lays them on a pan that has begun to walk across a stove. It was warm. Not from the lamp. Warm in the middle, where the street was.

The next morning I went out to the city. The rain had finally come, and Kolkata was a black mirror of roofs and puddles. I took the route Mirzapur Road had made for itself on the map, not the route I knew. It led me through lanes I had passed a hundred times and seen only once. At the corner of the fish market, the road I had been taught to draw ended in a wall. But the map, which I carried under my arm in an oilskin case, said it did not end. The inked line went on, through the wall, along a narrow passage between two houses, and stopped at the back of the Government Printing Press.

I stood in the wet and looked at the building. It was a plain brick wall, whitewashed, dry even in the rain. A drain ran at its foot. A cat watched me from the edge of a tile roof. I went round to the narrow passage the map had drawn. It was so narrow that a cart could not turn in it. A washerman was beating a cloth against a stone. A boy sat on a crate watching a lizard. No one looked at me. I stepped into the gap. It was not dark, exactly. It was the gray of a room where no one has been for a long time. At the end stood the wall of the printing press. There was no door. There was no gate. There was no place for Mirzapur Road to go.

And yet, when I held the map up against the light, the line on the paper did not end. It stopped at a tiny square drawn on the back wall of the building, and in the middle of the square was a mark I had not made: a small, neat door.

I stood there until the rain ran through my shoes. When I came back to the map room, the rain had stopped and the lamp in my corner had burned low. I opened the case and laid the map on the board. Mirzapur Road had not moved while I had been in the city. It had stayed where I had left it, and that frightened me more. It was waiting. The line ran through the fish market, through the narrow passage, and ended at the tiny square on the back wall. The small door in the centre of the square was still drawn there. I stared at it. I took my pen and, because I am a draughtsman and could not bear an unexplained mark on a sheet, I made a tiny key next to it. I wrote: “Door, unaccounted for.”

The pen had hardly dried when the lamp went out.

I did not move. I knew which wall was behind me: the bare plaster wall of the map room, the wall the map now said was not bare. I put my hand into the dark and found it. It was warm. It was smooth. It was a door.

The first time Mirzapur Road moved on my map, I blamed the heat.

The room above the Government Printing Press was a long, low box of a place, smelling of lampblack, pumice, and the particular stale sweetness of paper left too long in the sun. It was the third week of June, 1893, and the monsoon had not yet broken. The ceiling fan clicked in its slow circle. Outside, a water-carrier called for water in a voice that sounded like it had been dragged down a well. On the board before me, the new map of North Calcutta lay pinned at its four corners, a blue-white sheet of paper no bigger than a dining table.

My map was nearly finished. I had been hired to redraw the quarter between College Street and the old fish market for the drainage survey, a job considered too delicate for a junior draughtsman and too dull for a senior one. My father had been a leveller in the Bengal Survey. He died leaving me a theodolite, a set of brass dividers, and the conviction that if a thing would not stand still, it had not been measured carefully enough. I had measured Mirzapur Road twice. I had checked its bearing against the old plans, its width against the footnotes in my father's field book, its corners against the positions of three temples, a clockmaker's shop, and the back gate of the Serampore Mission house.

At five o'clock I had inked the final line. I had let it dry under a blotter. I had trimmed the lamp. At eleven o'clock, when I looked up from copying a contour line, Mirzapur Road stood six millimetres to the north of where I had left it.

I touched the table. The board was steady. I touched the map. The paper was smooth, taut, unmarked. The ink was dry. I lifted my dividers and measured from the fixed line of College Street to the moved line of Mirzapur. Six millimetres. I measured again. Six millimetres. I looked at the four brass pins. They were in the same holes. I looked at my hand. It was open, empty, and very clean.

Then I did what my father would have done. I stopped being frightened and began taking notes.

By twelve, Mr. Hartley had found his way up from the lower office with a tin cup of tea and the look of a man who expected trouble to be his. He was an assistant surveyor, a small Englishman with a mustache that tried to look important and usually failed. He set the cup down on my T-square. I moved it.

"You have lost the scale, Amala," he said.

"No, sir."

"You have. That whole block is leaning."

"Only Mirzapur Road is leaning, sir. The rest of the city is exactly where I put it."

He leaned over the sheet. The lamp flared between us. I saw his mouth tighten. When a man like Mr. Hartley saw something he did not like, he made it smaller.

"The paper has curled," he said.

"The paper is pinned at four corners."

"Heat does strange things."

"It is June, sir. It does strange things every day. But it has not moved a single house, a single lane, or a single temple on this map. It has moved Mirzapur Road."

He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, in the tone he used when he meant to be kind and succeeded only in being tired, "A street does not move, Miss Roy."

"Not yet," I said.

He stared at me. I would have given a good deal to unsay it. But the words were in the room already, and the lamp oil smelt sharper than before.

Dwarkanath Sen, the old clerk, came in with the field book. He had a face full of folds, like a map that had been folded and unfolded so often it had begun to hold creases for their own sake. He put the book on the board and opened it to Mirzapur.

"The old survey put the road here," he said, tapping a line in the margin. "Three houses south of where you have it now. But the houses are where they have always been. The fishmonger is at the same corner. The clockmaker has the same broken window. The road is where you see it."

"Is it?" I asked. "Have you walked it this week?"

"Why would I walk a road?"

"Because you are telling me it is still there."

He looked at me as if I had suggested he walk into the Ganges. "It is a road, Miss Roy. Roads are not things you lose."

"Then perhaps it is something else," I said. "Something that has learned to be a road."

I sent him away with the old plans and an order to fetch the 1878 proof copies from the lower vault. I told Mr. Hartley I needed to compare the sheet with the original tracings. He gave me a look that said he would be back before I had time to invent a second impossibility, and then he was gone, his boots tapping softly on the stairs.

When I was alone, I took a fine pencil and made four small crosses on the board, exactly outside the four corners of the map. I put my brass ruler across Mirzapur Road and left it there. Then I walked down to the tea room, drank two cups of strong black tea, and listened to the printer's boys argue about cricket.

When I came up, the ruler was where I had left it. Mirzapur Road had moved another four millimetres east. The line passed through the shadow of the ruler as if the ruler had been a window and the street a bird. I wrote the time in my notebook: 1:17. I wrote the distance: four millimetres. I wrote the direction: east by north. I wrote, in letters so small they looked like insects, "It is not the paper."

The second night it moved again. The third night, I did not go down for tea. I stayed in the room with the door barred, the lamp burning, and a cup of cold water on the table. At one o'clock I heard it. I had thought it was the street, but I had not known the street made a sound. It was not a footstep. It was not a wheel. It was a soft scraping, like the slow passage of a chisel across wet plaster, and it came from under the floor, from the wall, from the paper itself. I looked down. Mirzapur Road was sliding a little to the south, toward the line of Bakergunge Street. I did not breathe. I lifted the map with both hands, as one lifts a pan that has begun to walk across a stove. It was warm. Not from the lamp. Warm in the middle, where the street was.

I took the route Mirzapur Road had made for itself on the map, not the route I knew. It led me through lanes I had passed a hundred times and seen only once. At the corner of the fish market, the road I had been taught to draw ended in a wall. But the map, which I carried under my arm in an oilskin case, said it did not end. The inked line went on, through the wall, along a narrow passage between two houses, and stopped at the back of the Government Printing Press.

I stood in the wet and looked at the building. It was a plain brick wall, whitewashed, dry even in the rain. A drain ran at its foot. A cat watched me from the edge of a tile roof. I went round to the narrow passage the map had drawn. It was so narrow that a cart could not turn in it. A washerman was beating a cloth against a stone. A boy sat on a crate watching a lizard. The room above the Government Printing Press was a long, low box of a place, smelling of lampblack, pumice, and the particular stale sweetness of paper left too long in the sun. It was the third week of June, 1893, and Kolkata had not yet learned to be called Kolkata in official documents. The ceiling fan clicked in its slow circle. Outside, a water-carrier called for water in a voice that sounded like it had been dragged down a well. On the board before me, the new map of North Kolkata lay pinned at its four corners, a blue-white sheet of paper no bigger than a dining table.

My map was nearly finished. I had been hired to redraw the quarter between College Street and the old fish market for the drainage survey, a job considered too delicate for a junior draughtsman and too dull for a senior one. My father had been a leveller in the Bengal Survey. He died leaving me a theodolite, a set of brass dividers, and the conviction that if a thing would not stand still, it had not been measured carefully enough. I had measured Mirzapur Road twice. I had checked its bearing against the old plans, its width against the footnotes in my father's field book, its corners against the positions of three temples, a clockmaker's shop, and the back gate of the Serampore Mission house.

At five o'clock I had inked the final line. I had let it dry under a blotter. I had trimmed the lamp. At eleven o'clock, when I looked up from copying a contour line, Mirzapur Road stood six millimetres to the north of where I had left it.

I touched the table. The board was steady. I touched the map. The paper was smooth, taut, unmarked. The ink was dry. I lifted my dividers and measured from the fixed line of College Street to the moved line of Mirzapur. Six millimetres. I measured again. Six millimetres. I looked at the four brass pins.
